title: Khusrau and Shirin and the Fisherman

keywords: khusrau and shirin and the fisherman
full_text:
King Khusrau of ancient Persia sat in his summer pavilion beside a cool lake, accompanied by his beloved queen, the fair Shirin. An honest fisherman approached the royal pavilion and presented the monarch with a magnificent, glistening fish of enormous size, freshly caught from the mountain waters.

Khusrau was so delighted by the splendid gift that he commanded his treasurer to reward the fisherman with four thousand silver dirhams!

Queen Shirin, who possessed a sharp financial mind, whispered to the king: 'My lord, you have acted with excessive haste. If you bestow four thousand dirhams for a single fish, whenever you reward your generals and viziers with such a sum, they will grumble, saying: "The king values our services no more than a fisherman’s catch!"'

Khusrau frowned: 'It is unseemly for a monarch to withdraw a gift once granted. What can be done?'

Shirin smiled cleverly: 'Summon the fisherman and ask him: "Is this fish male or female?" If he says male, say: "We required a female fish," and if he says female, say: "We required a male fish!" Thus you may lawfully revoke the reward.'

The fisherman was called back before the throne. Khusrau asked with royal gravity: 'Tell me, fisherman: is this splendid fish male or female?'

The fisherman, perceiving the trap with lightning wit, bowed low and answered: 'May heaven preserve the king! This fish is neither male nor female; it is an extraordinary creature that partakes of the nature of both, created by the heavens especially for the royal table of Khusrau!'

Khusrau laughed heartily at the fisherman’s brilliant reply and immediately ordered another four thousand dirhams to be added to his purse!

As the fisherman departed carrying the heavy bag of eight thousand dirhams, a single silver coin slipped through a hole and fell into the dust. The fisherman bent down, picked it up, and wiped it upon his sleeve.

Shirin exclaimed: 'Look at the miser! Even with eight thousand dirhams, he cannot leave a single coin for the palace servants!'

Khusrau demanded: 'Why did you grudge a single coin to the earth?'

The fisherman bowed: 'Heaven forbid that I should be a miser, sire! But upon that coin is stamped the sacred image of the King; I could not bear that the feet of men should trample upon the likeness of my sovereign!'

Enchanted by his incomparable tact, Khusrau commanded a third reward of four thousand dirhams, proving that a quick tongue and courteous mind can conquer all the subtleties of courts.
moral: Sharp wit, polite presence of mind, and eloquent speech can turn a king's test into double fortune.
